lead.headline: Eisenkot gets the mandate to form Israel's next government, but the numbers are hard
lead.standfirst: President Herzog asked Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot to try to build a coalition, and as the new Knesset is sworn in today, nobody yet has a clear path to 61 seats.
paragraphs: On November 8, President Isaac Herzog gave Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, the job of forming the next government, according to the Times of Israel. Sixty-seven of the Knesset's 120 members had recommended him: a Jewish-led bloc of 48 and an Arab-led bloc of 19. Benjamin Netanyahu is recommended by 46, and Likud is the largest single party with 27 seats. A government needs 61 votes to win a confidence vote. Eisenkot said he wants a national emergency government and that it will take what he called creative and unconventional political acts. He listed four principles for any partner: Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, the values of the Declaration of Independence, mandatory national service for all, and recognizing Hamas as a terror group and committing to its destruction.

The obstacle is arithmetic. According to the report, Arab parties have said they will back an Eisenkot government or at least not vote against it, while some members of his Jewish bloc say they will not join a government that depends on those votes. Reported options include a minority government or bringing in the Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties, long allies of Netanyahu. Times of Israel reports that Avigdor Liberman of Yisrael Beytenu has cleared Eisenkot to approach the Haredim and that the two agreed on a Knesset speaker, with Eisenkot possibly taking that role while he builds a government. The clock: Eisenkot has up to 42 days. If he fails, Netanyahu gets 28 days, and if neither succeeds, 61 members can still agree on a third candidate within 21 days, after which the process leads to new elections. Eisenkot rejects that outcome. The 26th Knesset, with 46 first-time members, is sworn in today.

briefs.headline: Without a government, the IDF's planning and funding stall
briefs.text: Ynet reports the defense establishment is short about NIS 25 billion: Netanyahu agreed on June 30 to transfer NIS 40 billion, but only NIS 15 billion has arrived. Debts to defense industries are approaching NIS 20 billion, and the report warns shell and interceptor production could be disrupted. Decisions on new refueling aircraft and helicopters have been pushed to summer 2027.

briefs.headline: Police reportedly see little evidence behind Shin Bet's election-interference probe
briefs.text: Shin Bet chief David Zini asked the attorney general to approve questioning of Arab lawmakers over alleged foreign interference in last month's election. Channel 12 reported a preliminary police assessment found no security offenses and few criminal ones; the Channel 12 findings are unconfirmed. Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara said she saw nothing that would even remotely affect the election result, and no decision on the probe has been made.

briefs.headline: Trump says the Iran war is militarily over; Netanyahu reportedly wants it resumed
briefs.text: Trump said there is a good chance of a deal with Iran and that the US will not launch a new offensive for now. The Financial Times, cited by Times of Israel, reports Netanyahu is calling Trump every day to urge resuming the war, while another source said there is no active push at the moment. Iran's Mohsen Rezaei rejected talk of negotiations and said the US should accept Iran's seven conditions.

briefs.headline: Storms flood Gaza tents; Israel and the Board of Peace disagree on aid
briefs.text: Heavy rain flooded tens of thousands of displacement tents in Gaza. The IDF says winter supplies were delivered, while the US-backed Board of Peace says Israel must send more aid and also blames Hamas for refusing to disarm.

items.label: US news
items.headline: Trump says no new Iran offensive for now, citing talks and Gulf allies
paragraphs: President Trump said the US will not launch a renewed offensive against Iran for the time being, writing on Truth Social that there is positive momentum and that Gulf allies want to avoid escalation. He told reporters the war is militarily effectively over, that there is a good chance of a deal, and that the US remains locked and loaded. He described continued US efforts to blockade Iran's ports and block overland smuggling routes.

Trump met Qatar's prime minister on Monday, who said they discussed ways to progress the US-Iran talks. Iran's security council chief Mohsen Rezaei publicly dismissed reports of talks and told the US to accept Iran's seven conditions. Separately, a Republican lawmaker moved to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the war, according to Times of Israel.
items.why_it_matters: It sets whether the region heads back to open war or toward a deal, and it feeds directly into oil prices and markets.

items.label: Stock market
items.headline: Stocks jump as oil falls, with a key inflation report due today
paragraphs: On Monday the Dow rose 1,104 points (2.2%), the S&P 500 about 2.4% and the Nasdaq 2.7%, CNBC reported. Oil helped: US crude fell more than 4% to about $86.85 a barrel after Trump called fresh Iran attacks highly unlikely. Nvidia fell 4% and sat out the rally after CEO Jensen Huang confirmed an affair with a woman US intelligence suspects of being a Chinese spy, prompting a board investigation and a requested congressional hearing.

Today at 8:30 a.m. ET the October consumer price index (CPI), the main measure of inflation, is due. Economists polled by Dow Jones expect prices up 0.3% on the month, 0.2% excluding food and energy. The 10-year Treasury yield is about 4.88%, and Edward Jones expects the Fed to raise rates another quarter point in December.
items.why_it_matters: With the Fed considering more rate hikes, one inflation number can swing stocks, mortgage rates and the whole market mood.

stories.headline: OpenAI says its AI agents found 948 ways to take over Linux machines, then helped patch them
stories.standfirst: An automated pipeline hunted for kernel bugs, wrote working exploits, and proposed fixes, at a claimed cost of about $1.2 million.
stories.what_happened: In a November 4 report, OpenAI says a prototype pipeline of AI agents analyzed 2,308 candidate flaws in the Linux kernel, reproduced 1,724 of them, and produced exploits for 948 distinct bugs that let an ordinary user become administrator. The run used $1,213,430 in API credits, which OpenAI calls an upper bound. Human researchers review each finding before it is reported to maintainers. OpenAI says that while the campaign was running 61 of the bugs were already patched upstream and 43 had staged patches.
stories.what_it_means: The kernel is the core of the operating system, and a bug that lets any user gain full control is called a privilege escalation. Finding these used to need rare human experts. OpenAI is showing that agents can do the whole loop: find the bug, prove it is real by exploiting it, and write the fix. OpenAI also says that in an earlier run, 20 of 200 apparent successes actually exploited a different bug than assigned, so each exploit is now checked against its intended flaw.
stories.why_it_matters: Attackers can use the same techniques, so defenders get patches faster only if maintainers can keep up with the volume. For someone working near kernels and drivers, such as network stacks, it means bugs in that code will be found at machine speed. Note that OpenAI is keeping some technique details back, and these are the company's own figures.
terms: Privilege escalation
A bug that lets a normal user gain full administrator control of a computer.
Exploit
A program that takes advantage of a bug to make it do something harmful.
Kernel
The core of the operating system that manages hardware and memory for every program.

stories.headline: MIT researchers let an AI model edit another model's weights directly
stories.standfirst: Instead of retraining, a frontier model read a small network's numbers and rewrote some of them, and one small model's math score jumped from 7.9% to 48.1%.
stories.what_happened: A paper-style blog post from MIT CSAIL (Takehi, Teoh, Zhang and Khattab) describes weight-space programming: a general-purpose model reads a network's raw weights as text and edits or writes them from a plain-language goal. The authors anonymize the model as GPT-6 Astra. Editing 131,072 weights (0.016%) of Qwen3.5-0.8B to stop endless reasoning loops raised MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%, and answers hitting the token limit fell from 93% to 33%. In a driving game, one edit changed 3.5% of the weights and succeeded in all 1,024 episodes, where the conventionally trained policy never succeeded in 256.
stories.what_it_means: A neural network is just a huge table of numbers called weights. Normally you adjust them slowly through training. Here a smart model reads the table like a program, finds what is causing a failure, and changes a few entries by hand, like a mechanic opening the engine instead of rebuilding the car. The Qwen fix worked because that small model often got stuck looping, so removing the loop unlocked ability it already had.
stories.why_it_matters: If it scales, models could be debugged and customized in minutes without training runs. The authors are clear about limits: it gave no gain on Gemma 3 270M, which rarely loops, so editing removes obstacles but cannot add missing skills. Most experiments are small, results depend on tools and compute budgets, and the work is early and self-reported.
terms: Weights
The numbers inside a neural network that store everything it has learned.
MATH-500
A set of 500 math problems used to score models.
Gradient descent
The usual training method that nudges weights a little at a time to reduce errors.

stories.headline: Moonshot releases Kimi K3.1 Pro, a 2.8-trillion-parameter model with open weights
stories.standfirst: A huge but efficient model that only uses about 104 billion parameters per word, with a one-million-token context.
stories.what_happened: Moonshot AI published Kimi K3.1 Pro on Hugging Face under its own custom license. The model card says it has 2.8 trillion total parameters with about 104 billion active per token, uses a mixture-of-experts design with 896 experts (16 picked per token), accepts text and images, and handles about 1 million tokens of context. It is trained with 4-bit weights. Moonshot reports scores such as 94.2 on GPQA-Diamond and 79.6 on OSWorld V2.1; these are Moonshot's own claims, and some comparison numbers come from other vendors' reports.
stories.what_it_means: Mixture-of-experts means the model is like a hospital with 896 specialists: for each word it calls only 16 of them (plus 2 always-on), so it runs far cheaper than its total size suggests. Open weights means you can download the numbers and run it yourself, though this license has custom terms.
stories.why_it_matters: For inference engineers, such a model still needs large multi-GPU systems and fast networking between them, since experts live on different GPUs. Moonshot recommends the serving engines vLLM and SGLang. It also shows open models staying close to the proprietary frontier on agent and coding tests, by the vendor's own measure.
terms: Mixture of experts
A model made of many specialist sub-networks where only a few are used for each token.
Active parameters
The part of the model actually used to process each token.
Context window
How much text the model can consider at once; 1 million tokens is roughly several long books.

stories.headline: inferd: an open-source engine built to run many AI agents at once on a Mac
stories.standfirst: It applies data-center serving tricks, such as continuous batching and speculative decoding, to Apple Silicon.
stories.what_happened: Incept5 released inferd, an experimental Apache-2.0 inference engine for Apple Silicon. It serves one model to many concurrent agents using continuous batching, speculative decoding, an 8-bit KV cache stored in pages, a prefix cache that shares one agent's context with others, and an SSD tier for contexts that don't fit in memory. The project reports 849 tokens per second for 64 agents on 16k contexts on a Mac Studio M5 Ultra with a 27B model. These are the authors' own benchmarks, and they say other engines are faster for a single stream.
stories.what_it_means: When an AI agent works, it keeps a large memory of the conversation so far, called the KV cache. With many agents, those memories are the bottleneck. inferd saves common starting contexts once and lets many agents reuse them, and parks idle ones on disk, like keeping files on a shelf instead of the desk.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows that techniques from big inference servers are moving down to desktop machines, so a small team could run a fleet of coding agents locally. It is young software with no independent reviews yet.
terms: Continuous batching
Serving many requests together and letting new ones join as others finish.
Speculative decoding
A small model guesses several tokens ahead and the big model checks them in one go.
KV cache
The stored intermediate results for earlier tokens so they are not recomputed.

nature.headline: He spent a year on 'Mars': a NASA science officer emerges from a mock mission
nature.standfirst: After 378 days in a simulated Mars habitat, an engineer describes what a long isolated mission is like.
paragraphs: Nature's news team interviewed a NASA science officer who has just completed a 378-day simulated Mars mission: a year-plus living and working as if on another planet, though still on Earth. The full article is behind a login, so this summary rests only on Nature's published description.

According to that description, the engineer talks about the experience and about a two-week stretch with no contact with the outside world. Missions like this let space agencies study how people cope with isolation and communication gaps before sending real crews on the much longer trip to Mars.
key_points: What happened: a science officer finished a 378-day simulated Mars mission.
How it was done: crew members lived in a simulation, including a two-week period cut off from the outside world.
Why it matters: it tests how humans handle isolation, a key challenge for real Mars trips.
terms: Simulated mission
An Earth-based exercise that copies the conditions of a space trip, such as a sealed habitat and delayed contact.

study.title: Sequence numbers, ACKs and retransmission: how TCP knows what arrived
study.big_idea: TCP numbers every byte it sends, the receiver keeps telling the sender the next byte number it expects, and if that answer stops advancing the sender sends the missing bytes again.
background: The network underneath TCP, IP, is a best-effort service. Packets can be lost, duplicated, delayed or delivered out of order. TCP's job is to hide that and give the application a clean stream of bytes. To do that it needs a way to say which bytes arrived.

TCP cuts your data into pieces called segments. The largest chunk of application data in one segment is the MSS, typically 1460 bytes on Ethernet (a 1500-byte packet minus 40 bytes of IP and TCP headers). Think of mailing a book in numbered envelopes: if the recipient says 'I have everything up to page 300', you know exactly what to resend.
steps: At connection setup each side picks a random starting sequence number (the ISN). The SYN flag itself uses up one number.
Every byte of data has a sequence number. A segment carries the number of its first byte in the header, a 32-bit field. A segment with 1460 bytes starting at 1000 covers bytes 1000 to 2459.

The receiver replies with an ACK containing the next byte it expects, here 2460. ACKs are cumulative: 'everything before 2460 is safe'. The receiver usually acknowledges every second full segment, or after a short delay, to save packets.
The sender keeps a copy of unacknowledged data and starts a retransmission timer (RTO) for it. If the ACK number moves past the data, the copy is freed and the timer is reset or stopped.
If the timer expires first, the sender retransmits the oldest unacknowledged segment and doubles the timer (exponential backoff), so a congested network is not flooded with retries.
If a segment arrives out of order, the receiver holds it and repeats the same ACK number. The sender notices repeated identical ACKs, which lead to faster recovery methods covered in a later lesson.
study.example: A client sends 3 segments starting at byte 1000, and the second is lost. The server receives bytes 1000 to 2459 and ACKs 2460. It then gets the third segment, which starts at 3920, but it cannot ACK past the gap, so it ACKs 2460 again. The client sees ACK 2460 stuck while the data it sent goes beyond, and eventually it resends the segment starting at 2460. Once that arrives the server ACKs 5380 in one go, covering all three segments.
study.why_xlio: A user-space TCP stack like XLIO has to implement all of this itself: tracking sequence numbers per connection, holding unacknowledged data until it is ACKed, and running retransmission timers, work the kernel normally does. Because zero-copy sends keep user buffers in place until ACKed, the retransmission state also decides when an application's buffer can be reused.
numbers: 32 bits, so it wraps after 4 GiB of data
study.pitfall: A common misconception is that sequence numbers count packets. They count bytes, which is why the ACK number tells you exactly how much data arrived, regardless of how it was split into segments. Another is that an ACK means the application read the data; it only means the receiver's TCP stack has it.
terms: Segment
One TCP packet's worth of data plus its header.
ACK
Acknowledgment: a message telling the sender the next byte number the receiver expects.
RTT
Round-trip time: how long a message takes to go to the other side and the answer to come back.
RTO
Retransmission timeout: how long the sender waits for an ACK before resending.
Exponential backoff
Doubling the wait after each failed attempt.
Cumulative ACK
An ACK that confirms all bytes before a given number.
study.question: Why does TCP not measure the round-trip time using a segment that was retransmitted?
study.answer: Because when an ACK arrives you cannot tell whether it answers the original send or the retransmission, so the measured time could be badly wrong. TCP's rule (Karn's algorithm) is to skip such samples for timing, and it keeps the backed-off timer until a fresh segment is acknowledged. Recap: TCP numbers bytes, the receiver says which byte comes next, and a stuck ACK or an expired timer triggers a resend.
